# Asset sources

For licences, receipts and credits of third-party assets, and where free game art, icons, palettes, plugins and animations come from.

## Core

- Licences: CC0 needs nothing (credit is a courtesy). CC-BY and OGA-BY need the credit the author asks for. BY-SA and GPL make the derived asset carry the same licence; GPL art in a closed game needs the user's decision. NC never goes into paid, monetised or commercial work. Quote a custom or unclear licence verbatim to the user rather than summarising it.
- Each grabbed asset gets a receipt `<asset-id>.json` beside its files (`source`, `id`, `title`, `url`, `authors`, `license`, `licenseUrl`, `attribution`, `acquiredAt`, `files`) and a line in the project's `CREDITS`: title, author, source URL, licence.
- `voyager assets search <words> [--type texture|hdri|model|icon|music|pack] [--source …]` searches Poly Haven (CC0 textures, HDRIs, models), ambientCG (CC0 materials, HDRIs), Kenney (CC0 packs), game-icons.net and Incompetech; `voyager assets download <source>:<id> [--resolution 2k]` saves under `assets/<source>/<id>/` with the receipt and the `CREDITS` line. Poly Haven asks that users are told its assets come from Poly Haven.
- Kenney (kenney.nl): CC0 whole packs (2D, 3D, UI, audio, textures); search matches pack names and categories only. Packs include `License.txt`.
- Animated CC0 sets: Quaternius [Ultimate Animated Character Pack](https://quaternius.com/packs/ultimatedanimatedcharacter.html) and [Ultimate Animated Animal Pack](https://quaternius.com/packs/ultimateanimatedanimals.html), Kenney [Animated Characters Protagonists](https://kenney.nl/assets/animated-characters-protagonists), and three.js [RobotExpressive](https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/tree/dev/examples/models/gltf/RobotExpressive). fal’s [Meshy](https://fal.ai/models/meshy/v7.1/image-to-3d/api) `meshy/v7.1/image-to-3d` auto-rigs generated humanoids with `enable_rigging: true`; animation presets use `enable_animation: true` and `animation_action_id`.
- game-icons.net: CC BY 3.0 (a few authors CC0), credited per icon's author. Each SVG is a black square path under a white icon path; recolour or drop them via `fill`.
- Incompetech: Kevin MacLeod's music, CC BY 4.0 with his credit text; fetch single tracks only.
- Lospec: `https://lospec.com/palette-list/<slug>.json` returns name, author (sometimes empty; the palette page names the creator) and hex colours. Credit "<palette> by <author> (Lospec)".
- Godot Asset Library: keyless JSON at `godotengine.org/asset-library/api/asset?filter=…&godot_version=4.3` (without `godot_version` it returns nothing); `cost` holds the licence, `/asset/<id>` gives `download_url`. Plugins and scripts, not art. The new Godot Asset Store (beta, no public API) is replacing it.
- OpenGameArt: no API. Search pages (`/art-search-advanced?keys=…`) only; robots.txt sets a 10 s crawl delay and disallows `/search/`. Licences (often several, including SA and GPL) and the attribution text are on each content page.
- Mixamo: Adobe's terms forbid access other than through its interface and any data mining, so the user downloads in their own browser; Voyager imports and rigs the FBX. Raw characters and animations are not redistributable.
- itch.io: no search API (every endpoint needs auth and covers your own account); tag pages have RSS (`itch.io/game-assets/free/tag-<tag>.xml`) without licences. Licences are free text per page; the user downloads, and pays where needed.

# Godot

`voyager godot --help` lists the commands; `voyager godot start --help` shows
operations, flags and the scenario file shape. Use Voyager's pinned engine
(`godot status`, `godot setup`), never a Godot found on PATH. Start a new game with
`godot create` in an empty folder; the starters are editable, so read their scripts.

## Assets

`godot start --operation asset --asset '{…}'` converts a source into a validated,
cached project asset (model→GLB, image→PNG, audio→Ogg Vorbis, cinematic→Theora) and
lists it in `game-assets.json`. Fields: `id` (lowercase slug), `source`, `kind`
(`model|image|audio|cinematic`), `provenance` (where it came from), `dependencies`
(include a .blend's linked libraries), `width`/`height` (image size), `loop` (audio),
`maxTriangles`, `maxMaterials`, `maxDimension`, `requiredAnimations`, `pivot`
(`center`/`base` check the origin; they do not move it), `collisionHint` (metadata
only; add collision shapes yourself), `transparency` (`required|opaque|preserve`),
`preview` (model/image render; needs a display), `style`, `blender`. Game code loads
them with `preload("res://game_assets.gd").get_asset(id)`, which applies `loop`.
Importing files into `res://` directly also works.

## Playtests

`godot start --operation test --scenario file.json` runs the main scene under a
development runner that sends real input events. Each step holds one key, action or
mouse input for `frames`; a step without input waits. `expect` checks `snapshot()`
fields after the step; `until` ends the step when they match and fails if `frames`
run out; `assert` checks a node property (`scope: "node"`) or snapshot field
(`"state"`); `invariants` are checked every tick. Screenshots need `rendered: true`;
`recording: true` also writes an AVI (at most 36,000 requested frames). Results are in the job's `report.json`. For a
test the scenario format can't express, write your own Godot test script.

The main scene can provide these; they are plain game code and ship in exports:

```gdscript
signal gameplay_event(event_name: String, data: Dictionary)  # JSON-compatible data
func snapshot() -> Dictionary                # state scenarios check
func objectives() -> Array[Dictionary]       # {id, label, progress, required, complete}
func interactables() -> Array[Dictionary]    # {id, label, node, available}
var save_path                                # runner points it at a per-run file
```

Game logic must not detect the runner, and tests never read the user's real saves.

---
name: make-game
description: "Build, change and playtest desktop games in Godot, LÖVE, Pygame, Bevy, Defold or GameMaker."
applications:
  - id: godot
    role: primary
  - id: unity
    role: alternative
  - id: love
    role: primary
  - id: pygame
    role: primary
  - id: bevy
    role: primary
  - id: defold
    role: primary
  - id: gamemaker
    role: primary
voyager:
  schemaVersion: 1
  craft: [asset-sources]
---

Revisions keep their project's engine. New games honor user choice and saved
Gaming preference; otherwise ask which engine they prefer. For someone new to
game-making, Phaser (2D in the browser), three.js (3D in the browser) and Godot
(desktop 2D or 3D) cover most games. Unity or Unreal suit teams already using them.
Voyager also supports PixiJS, Babylon.js, PlayCanvas, KAPLAY, LÖVE, Pygame, Bevy,
Defold and GameMaker (plus Unity, Unreal and Roblox); any can be the better fit
for what the user wants. Use `develop-unity` for Unity, `develop-unreal` for Unreal,
`develop-roblox` for Roblox, `make-web-game` for browser games, and `make-x-game`
for games played inside an X post. For another named, saved or existing engine,
use its native APIs, project tools and computer use; no dedicated skill is required.
Do not run the Godot-specific commands or starter initialization below against
those projects. Never switch engines merely because a dedicated adapter is absent.

LÖVE, Pygame and native Bevy games run in desktop windows, outside the preview pane.
Defold builds outside its editor with Bob (Java); GameMaker CLI builds need Igor,
its installed runtime and licence setup. Neither toolchain is bundled with Voyager.

A Godot game uses Voyager's pinned engine and commands; read [references/godot.md](references/godot.md) before changing its code, assets or tests.

Generate the characters, props, textures and backgrounds with make-image, and 3D
models through choose-media-model (Tripo, Meshy, TRELLIS); mini-flows `game-asset-pack`
and `sprite-directions` cover sets and facings. Make them game-ready: transparent, one
style across a set, target sizes, atlases. Draw art in code only for a prototype the user
asked for or when no paid generation is available, and say so. Regenerate only changed
assets and dependencies.
A rigged 3D character with clothes or several body types follows edit-in-blender's
[rigged characters](../edit-in-blender/references/game-characters.md) guide.
Test with a [Godot-only playtest](references/godot.md#playtests); a changed source revision needs retesting.

After export, launch the executable outside the source folder, exercise the core
loop, and verify it has no development test dependency. Finish with controls,
evidence and artifact paths, unresolved issues, and exactly which host and target
were tested. Do not equate a green import with a fun or finished game, or publish
a game without the user's instruction.
